Ranchers from the surrounding parts of Texas and Mexico drive their cattle into the city to send them on their long journey to the north, east, and west of the United States. Take on the role of the ranchers of that time and bring your best cattle to El Paso to earn money and victory points. Hire more cowboys, builders, and engineers to get closer to your goals. Buy cattle to increase the value of your herd! Construct buildings to unlock more actions! Participate in the expansion of the railroad and secure the most attractive contracts! El Paso is mechanically based on its predecessors in the Great Western Trail trilogy. It can serve as an introduction to the series and is the perfect game for game nights when there is not enough time for its big brothers! Discover Board Game Arena Rules summary El Paso at the end of the 19th century: five railroad companies have connected the Sun City to their network and made it a major hub for the cattle trade. Take on the role of ranchers of that time and bring your best cattle to El Paso to earn money and victory points. Hire more cowboys, builders, and engineers to get closer to your goals. Contents 1 Display 2 Setup 3 Your Turn 3.1 Movement 3.2 Actions 3.2.1 Auxiliary Actions 3.2.2 Building Actions 3.2.3 El Paso Actions 3.3 Cleanup 4 Scoring Display The central display at the top features: • The map with El Paso (building A at the top) and a clockwise trail connecting Neutral buildings B-G and empty spaces, appearing as a dashed line. In the center of the map, there are trading posts with numbers above them and bonuses shown below them, as well as the orange Simmental cattle cards, with a counter how many are left. • Above the map, you see four train cards, each with 2-3 actions that can be accessed at building F. • Below the train (or on the right, depending on scaling), you see the stack of bonus tiles (with a bell icon) and three face-up tiles beside it, as well as the stack of objective tiles (with a horn icon) and, also, three face-up tiles beside it. These can be gained at building F. • Below the map (or on the right, depending on scaling), there is the building display, featuring the six types of buildings; each building has a counter showing how many are left. For details on the building cost, click the question mark icon. Buildings can be placed/replaced on the map at building E. • Below the buildings, there is the cattle market, featuring the four types of cattle, also showing how many of each type are left. Note the question mark icon that tells you how much each cattle card costs. Cattle can be acquired at building D. • Last, but not least, below the cattle market, you see the four types of workers and how many of each type are left. These can be hired at building B. Your personal play area features: • At the top, your draw pile, showing how many cards it contains, and your hand of cattle cards (four at the start). As the game progresses, your discard pile will be shown to the right of your hand. • Below that, on the left, you see your player board featuring 4 auxiliary actions on the left, of which 4 spaces are covered with a disc; in the middle, you see three bonuses you can unlock; and, on the right, you see your certificate track, which shows how many certificates you will be able to spend in El Paso (see El Paso action). • Finally, to the right of your player board, you see how many workers of each type you have at your disposal. Note that workers have bonuses printed at the top that you can use at any time on your turn (you will see a button in the status bar reminding you of that). The player panel in the side bar shows: • With live scoring enabled, your score below your username. • Below that: your cash (coin = $); your cards in hand; your herder’s ran

[Rating: 1/10] Fans of GWT would probably enjoy this. Me, I couldn't even tell that it was simplified, it was just as convoluted as the original. They probably took out [i]something[/i], but I can't tell what because the core is identically convoluted as before.

[Rating: 1/10] A mess of a game. Strips away many elements that elevate the original GREAT WESTERN TRAIL—e.g. the timing of the worker market, the trade-off of moving (or not moving) your train, the race for station master tiles, the strategic tax building placement relative to hazards—leaving behind the skeletal remains of a boring "deck builder" that has depressingly little player agency and whose core gameplay loop feels totally uninspired. To say nothing of the game's egregious imbalance: One of the early buildings is incredibly overpowered if placed in the position just outside of El Paso (I think 2a, t

[Rating: 1/10] At first I liked this game, but then I saw someone basically completely break the game on BGA and more than triple the other players scores by getting rid of cows, buying wild workers and then thinning their deck to the point where they created an almost infinite loop of just workers and then discarding workers for money with the free action and getting over 200 coins (40+ points) and basically breaking the game.  What a shame!!

[Rating: 1/10] Terrible game, the GWT trilogy is amazing, but El Paso seems to exist only for the money

[Rating: 2/10] Terrible components. I love all things GWT except this game is hot garbage. And gets boring fast. Will not play again.

But that one small improvement doesn't save this game from being a waste of time. [Rating: 3.5/10] Contains most of the moving parts that identify it as GWT, but no fun really remains.  cardboard discs and "cubes" are hilariously crappy components, though maybe that was just in the prototype i played?.  Still this would be a functional tool for the introduction / education of people who struggle to understand GWT 1e (and based on the existence of building 2A, this group somehow includes krenner/pfister?).  Should i even be rating this as a game for adults and not as the equivalent of a picture book?

[Rating: 3.5/10] This version stripped away a lot of the elements that made the original GWT so great. Workers as cards can make it very frustrating to take the actions you need if they don’t cycle through the deck quickly enough. And the solo bot is punishingly imbalanced, even on the easiest mode. Can’t really recommend this one.

[Rating: 4/10] Played a couple of times on BGA. It's, in essence, really a quick version of GWT. Captures the core element, leaves away all the nuances. The most innovative thing is that the employees also go into your deck, a really smooth card game, instead of a "big" game.

[Rating: 4/10] As a fan of the Great Western Trail series, I approached "Great Western Trail: El Paso" with high expectations. Unfortunately, the game turned out to be quite a disappointment for me.  "El Paso" offers a streamlined version of the familiar mechanics, packed into a smaller box, with simplified rules and a shorter playtime. However, these changes came at the cost of depth and the exciting feel that I valued so much in the previous entries. [Rating: 4/10] - Way too derivative (even more than Pirates of Maracaibo), loose and shallow. Total lack of interaction.

[Rating: 4/10] I have no idea why I would ever play this over one of the other GWT games. This simplified version basically strips the fun out of the game and you just go around and around in circles taking the same actions over and over. Not much room for creative strategies here that I saw (granted it's only 1 play, but it left me bored silly, so I have little desire to try again). Obviously not targeted at me:)

[Rating: 4/10] Wanted to enjoy this one but like Maracaibo/Pirates of Maracaibo just does not hit me right. For the decision space feels too limited unlike Mombasa, Boonlake and GWT. Caught in a similar feeling to that which I received from Oh My Goods. Pfister sings for me with deeper games.

[Rating: 4/10] There's only one viable strategy, it's too long, and extremely luck-based. One of the worst examples of simplifying a complicated game. [BGA]

[Rating: 4/10] The goal was clearly to make a faster, simpler game in the GWT series, and on that front it succeeds. Sadly, there’s little resemblance to what makes the series great.

[Rating: 4/10] I like the game, but the components could have been better. the rule book too, no appendix. you have to download it and print it out yourself.
